content: Tartrazine is one of the most widely used food additives and is particularly well-known among food colorants. These colorants are not only present in food products but are also commonly found in various medications. There has been ongoing debate regarding whether tartrazine exacerbates asthma symptoms. Some studies have suggested a positive association, particularly in individuals who exhibit cross-sensitivity to aspirin. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of tartrazine, either through exclusion from the diet or through controlled challenge, on the management of asthma. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted using the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register. Bibliographies of relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were also reviewed to identify additional studies. Authors of the identified RCTs were contacted to obtain further information. The search strategy is updated annually, with the most recent update being in February 2006. The inclusion criteria for this review were RCTs that involved oral administration of tartrazine as a challenge compared to a placebo, or dietary avoidance of tartrazine compared to a normal diet. Studies specifically focusing on allergic asthma were included. Additionally, studies addressing other allergic conditions, such as hay fever, allergic rhinitis, or eczema, were considered only if they provided separate results for participants with asthma. Both adult and pediatric populations with asthma or allergic asthma (e.g., sensitivity to aspirin or tartrazine-containing foods) were eligible for inclusion. The quality of the studies was independently assessed by two reviewers, and data were extracted for analysis. The outcomes were analyzed using RevMan version 4.1.1. Out of 94 abstracts identified, 20 were deemed potentially relevant. Of these, six studies met the inclusion criteria. However, only three studies presented their results in a format suitable for analysis, and none of the studies could be combined into a meta-analysis. Across all included studies, neither dietary exclusion of tartrazine nor tartrazine challenge significantly affected asthma outcomes. The authors concluded that the limited evidence available does not allow for definitive conclusions regarding the effects of tartrazine on asthma control. However, the six RCTs included in this review consistently found no significant benefit from routine tartrazine exclusion in the management of asthma. It is suggested that tartrazine exclusion may only be beneficial for a very small subset of individuals with confirmed sensitivity to this additive.
